Snare
snâr
n. (a trap for birds or beasts; rendering Hebrew pach and moqesh, Greek pagis)
From the Saxon snear, a cord. Hebrew pach is the fowler's net or snare, and moqesh is the bait-stick of a trap — the part that looks harmless and springs the mechanism — which is exactly the picture Scripture wants when it speaks of temptation.

Biblical Definition

Snare is a hidden trap, and every biblical use turns on concealment: a snare that could be seen would catch nothing. The Psalter promises deliverance from it as the first of God's protections: “Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence” (Psalm 91:3), and celebrates escape in the language of a bird that got free: “Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped” (Psalm 124:7) — note that the deliverance came by the breaking of the snare, not by the bird's strength. Proverbs identifies the commonest snare in a single line: “The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe” (Proverbs 29:25), which sets the two fears against each other and makes the fear of the LORD the antidote to the fear of men. Paul warns that office in the church has its own particular danger and requires a man's reputation outside the church as a safeguard: an overseer “must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil” (1 Timothy 3:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

A hidden trap, so called because it cannot be seen. Scripture's commonest snare is the fear of man; the deliverance in Psalm 124 comes by the snare being broken, not by the bird's own strength.

expand to see more

SNARE, n. [Sax. snear, a cord.] An instrument for catching animals, particularly birds, by the leg or neck.

2. Anything by which one is entangled and brought into trouble.

3. As a verb, to catch with a snare; to entangle; to bring into unexpected evil.

4. In Scripture, the fear of man bringeth a snare, Prov. 29.

5. Of the devil's trap; as, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil, 1 Tim. 3.

Key Scripture

Psalm 91:3 — "Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence."

Proverbs 29:25 — "The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe."

1 Timothy 3:7 — "Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil."

Psalm 124:7 — "Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped."

Modern Corruption

The fear of man is not usually recognised as sin at all; it passes for tact, prudence, or kindness. Proverbs calls it a snare and sets it against trust in the LORD as the direct alternative.

expand to see more

Proverbs 29:25 is among the most quietly convicting verses in Scripture because the sin it names is so respectable. Very few men will admit to being afraid of other men; they will say they are being wise, or keeping the peace, or choosing their battles. The verse does not allow the euphemisms. It calls the thing a snare, which means it is a trap and the man in it is caught, and it offers only one alternative — trust in the LORD. Peter denied his Lord to a servant girl, and Aaron made a calf because the people were set on it; both were snared this way.

The principle to recover is the mechanism a snare depends on. It works by being invisible, so a man does not decide to be trapped; he discovers he is. That is why Paul requires an overseer to have a good report from those outside the church — a life already exposed to unsympathetic eyes is much harder to snare. And Psalm 124:7 keeps the hope where Scripture always puts it: the bird did not out-fly the fowler, and the man does not out-think the devil. The snare is broken, and we are escaped.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pach is a fowler's snare or net, and moqesh the bait-stick that springs the trap. Greek pagis is a snare, and skandalon the trigger of a trap, hence a stumbling block.

expand to see more

Hebrew pach (H6341) — a snare, a bird trap; the snare of the fowler.

Hebrew moqesh (H4170) — the bait or trigger of a trap; the fear of man bringeth a snare.

Hebrew resheth (H7568) — a net; mine eyes are ever toward the LORD, for he shall pluck my feet out of the net.

Greek pagis (G3803) — a snare, a trap; the snare of the devil in 1 Timothy 3:7.

Greek skandalon (G4625) — the trigger stick of a trap, a stumbling block; the root of English scandal.

Usage

"Of deliverance promised: he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler (Psalm 91:3)."

"Of the commonest snare: the fear of man bringeth a snare (Proverbs 29:25)."

"Of the danger attending office: lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil (1 Timothy 3:7)."
